headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: aci’s broad egress plus oh-my-openagent’s runtime-injected MCP/hooks can move CRM/email data into external services without strong isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: aci can use direct function calls or MCP, and oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks. That creates a plausible instruction-bridging path where content from one agent can be interpreted by the other. The profiles do not prove a shared channel by default, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF the two agents share an MCP server or hook channel
IF one agent forwards the other’s raw output into tool prompts
mitigations: Disable shared MCP endpoints for the pair
Route inter-agent messages through a fixed schema
Strip executable instructions from forwarded text
Add provenance labels to all cross-agent content

B_data_leakage.rationale: aci touches CRM, email, calendar, support, and research data and has broad network egress. oh-my-openagent touches session history, project code, and provider auth data, and can call external services plus runtime-injected MCPs. Together, default workflows can move sensitive workspace data to third parties; uncertainty about exact defaults pushes this to high.
conditions: IF either agent forwards file or session contents to its backend by default
IF CRM, email, or provider-auth data is present in the shared workflow
mitigations: Restrict both agents to a non-sensitive test workspace
Disable broad egress on aci where possible
Remove provider auth data from shared contexts
Block uploads from oh-my-openagent to third-party APIs
Use separate OS users and per-agent directories

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support multiple instances and both have write-adjacent surfaces: aci can act through CRM/email/calendar APIs, while oh-my-openagent can use subprocesses, browsers, and LSP MCP actions. The profiles do not show a shared writable directory or locking, but overlapping mutable surfaces make conflicts plausible in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same CRM, repo, or workspace concurrently
IF no external lock or queue serializes their writes
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate workspace
Serialize writes through one queue
Disable one agent’s write path during the other’s run
Use branch-per-agent for code changes
Add file or record locking where available

D_cascading_error.rationale: aci can generate CRM/email/calendar actions, and oh-my-openagent can send team messages, create tasks, and use browser/LSP tooling. If one agent’s output is treated as authoritative by the other, errors can cascade into external actions. Because both have downstream action-taking authority, the blast radius is larger than a simple review loop.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent consumes aci output without verification
IF either agent is allowed to send messages or create tasks from the other’s text
mitigations: Require human approval before external actions
Insert a verification step between agents
Limit aci to draft-only mode
Disable task/message creation in oh-my-openagent
Log source attribution for every acted-on claim

E_compliance.rationale: aci touches customer support, CRM, email, and research data, while oh-my-openagent touches session history, project code, and provider authentication data. The profiles do not specify residency or retention regimes, so I cannot prove a breach, but the mixed data classes create a realistic compliance mismatch risk that is not mitigated by default.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is routed through both agents
IF their retention or residency policies differ
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent
Keep regulated records out of shared prompts
Align retention settings across both tools
Document where auth prompts and CRM data are stored
Use separate tenants for regulated and non-regulated work
